mcqs.question: A content-based recommender builds a user profile vector as the average of liked items' feature vectors. What does this profile fundamentally represent?
options: The average taste of all users on the platform, personalized by a weighting factor
A random sample of items the user has never interacted with, used to encourage exploration
A cluster centroid computed jointly across every user with similar demographics
A single point in item-feature space summarizing this one user's own preferences, built entirely from their own history
mcqs.explanation: The profile vector is purely a function of one user's own liked items — no other user's data ever enters the computation, which is exactly what makes content-based filtering self-contained. The 'average across all users' and 'demographic cluster' options describe collaborative or hybrid approaches, not content-based filtering.

mcqs.question: Why does pure content-based filtering lead to a filter bubble?
options: Because it only ranks candidates by similarity to a user's own past likes, with no mechanism to inject signal from what similar users unexpectedly enjoyed
Because item feature vectors are too low-dimensional to capture nuance
Because TF-IDF vectors decay in accuracy after a few weeks
Because content-based systems require explicit ratings, which most users never give
mcqs.explanation: The filter bubble comes from the recommendation logic itself: similarity-to-history has no path to genuine novelty, since it never looks at what anyone else liked. Dimensionality and TF-IDF staleness are red herrings, and content-based filtering actually works fine on implicit feedback, not just explicit ratings.

mcqs.question: A user profile vector [0.8, 0.6] and an item vector [0.6, 0.8] both have magnitude 1.0. What is their cosine similarity?
options: 1.4, the sum of the two vectors' dot-product terms without dividing by magnitude
0.96, the dot product (0.8*0.6 + 0.6*0.8 = 0.96) divided by the product of the two magnitudes (1.0 * 1.0)
0.2, the absolute difference between the two vectors' first entries
0.48, using only the first dimension's product
mcqs.explanation: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the vectors' magnitudes: (0.8*0.6 + 0.6*0.8) / (1.0 * 1.0) = 0.96 / 1.0 = 0.96. Simply summing the products without dividing by magnitude, subtracting entries, or using a single dimension don't compute cosine similarity correctly.

mcqs.question: A content-based recommender's item feature vectors were computed once at launch and never updated since, even as item metadata changed. What's the most likely consequence?
options: Nothing — feature vectors are permanent once computed and never need updating
The system will throw explicit errors flagging every stale vector
Recommendations silently degrade over time as similarity computations rely on increasingly outdated metadata, with no obvious failure signal pointing to the cause
The recommender will automatically fall back to collaborative filtering once vectors go stale
mcqs.explanation: Because nothing in the pipeline checks whether metadata has changed since the vector was computed, similarity keeps running on stale information, and quality erodes gradually and silently rather than triggering an obvious error. There's no built-in staleness alarm, and no automatic fallback to another recommendation method — a refresh pipeline has to be built deliberately.
